structured_output.ground: O you who have believed: when you rise to the prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe over your heads, and [wash] your feet up to the two ankle-bones. If you are in a state of major impurity (junub), purify yourselves. If you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you has come from the privy (al-ghāʾiṭ, literally 'the low ground'), or you have touched women, and you do not find water, then aim for clean, good earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. God does not want to lay any constraint (ḥaraj) upon you. He wants to purify you and to complete His favour upon you, so that you may be grateful.

triggers.how: rising 'to' (إلى) prayer: the body is set in motion toward a goal
B003 (resolve, setting out to undertake a matter) is heard in the same verb

findings.statement: 'When you rise to the prayer' is both the body standing up and the resolve to undertake it, and the washing that follows belongs to that movement.
findings.perceptible: The ablution happens between rising and arriving. The prayer starts from the moment the body gets up to go to it, not at the first takbir.

triggers.how: shared scene water.washing; the water that is later absent
contrast between making water flow and passing a hand over

findings.statement: Washing (ghasl) means making water run over a limb so that it carries the dirt away, and the ayah sets this against wiping (masḥ), where only a hand passes over.
findings.perceptible: The reader sees two gestures: water running down the face, hands and feet, and a lighter hand passing over the head. The ayah's rule rests on that difference in touch.

triggers.how: the face is named again in tayammum
aiming; و ج ه B002/B005 (direction, qibla, intent) are facets of the same root
neighbouring image of heading for the House

findings.statement: The face that is washed and wiped is also, in the root's own logic, the side one turns toward a direction (wijha, qibla) and toward intent (tawajjuh). What is cleansed first is the part that faces.
findings.perceptible: The ablution begins where orientation begins. The same word names the surface the water runs over and the direction that surface will be turned in prayer.

triggers.how: the ayah closes by denying constraint; ر ف ق B001 is gentleness, the opposite of harshness
ر و د B005 is glossed الرفق والمهل: the verb of God's wanting shares a branch defined by rifq
B003 (marfiq: what one benefits from, ease in a need) in the same word

findings.statement: The washing reaches up to the elbows (marāfiq), the joints one leans on. Their name comes from the root of gentleness (rifq), companionship and useful ease (marfiq), and the ayah later says God does not want constraint.
findings.perceptible: The limit of the washing is named by a word of leaning and ease. The sentence's legal boundary already carries the tone of its conclusion (no ḥaraj): the body is measured at the place where it rests.

triggers.how: same verb used again for tayammum
م س ح B009 names level, bare, smooth ground, the same terrain as ṣaʿīd
م س ح B011: covering the land by travel, the traveller crossing it

findings.statement: Masḥ means passing the hand over something and removing its trace. The same root names level bare ground and crossing the land on a journey, so the wet hand on the head and the dusty hand on the face in tayammum are one gesture.
findings.perceptible: The wiping with water and the wiping with earth are one motion with two materials. The traveller who has 'wiped the land' (crossed it) wipes his face with that same land.

triggers.how: B002: al-Kaʿba, the square raised House, is the same root
the House in the neighbourhood; in the surah the Kaʿba is named at 5:95 and 5:97
the washed face will turn toward that House

findings.statement: The feet are washed to the two kaʿbs, the ankle-bones that stand out on either side of the foot. The same word for a raised, protruding knot names the Kaʿba, the raised square House toward which the cleansed body turns.
findings.perceptible: For a reader who knows Kâbe only as a proper name, the lowest limit of the ablution and the House of prayer are heard as one shape, a raised, jutting form. The body's measure and the direction of prayer share a word.

triggers.how: the verb takes its object with بِ, as it does again in بِوُجُوهِكُمْ

findings.statement: 'Wipe over your heads' takes its object with the preposition bi-, as the touching of a surface, while 'wash your faces' takes a direct object.
findings.perceptible: Turkish 'başınızı meshedin' flattens the difference: water is laid over the whole face, but the hand only makes contact with the head (and with the face in tayammum). The head, the top of the body (رأس B001 'top of a thing'), gets the lightest touch.

triggers.how: with the genitive reading the feet attach to the wiping clause
with the accusative reading the feet return to the washing verb

findings.statement: With the accusative (arjulakum) the feet are washed like the face and hands. The mutawātir genitive (arjulikum) sets them beside the heads under wiping. In both, the feet are the last limb, measured to the ankle-bones.
findings.perceptible: The order face, hands, head, feet runs from top to bottom. The accusative reading jumps back over the head to the washing verb, and the grammar holds the washed limbs and the wiped limb in one line.

triggers.how: B003 (distancing, keeping apart, being a stranger) and B001 (side) are facets of the same root
the remedy that ends the state
the dictionary explains the name as avoiding the places of prayer

findings.statement: Junub names the ritual state, and the root's image is of someone set to one side, kept at a distance (the word that gives ecnebi, 'stranger'). Full purification brings that person back from the side to the place of prayer.
findings.perceptible: The state is spatial, not only a label of impurity. The person stands aside from prayer the way a stranger stands at the edge, and the washing is a return. Turkish cünüp keeps only the rule.

triggers.how: same root; God as agent, B005 inner cleansing
God's wanting is aimed at taṭhīr

findings.statement: The believers are told 'purify yourselves' (the reflexive-effortful taṭahhur), and the ayah ends with God's own intent 'to purify you' (causative taṭhīr). The one purification is their act and His purpose.
findings.perceptible: The washing is placed inside a larger movement: what the hand does to the limbs is what God is doing to the person. Physical cleansing and purity of the self are one line, from the human act to the divine will.

triggers.how: contrast with the plain washing command for the minor state

findings.statement: Iṭṭahharū is taṭahharū with its t assimilated and doubled. The form stresses deliberate, thorough self-purification, beyond the simple 'wash'.
findings.perceptible: The major state asks for a heavier, all-over act. The doubled consonant carries that thoroughness, and the Turkish 'temizlenin' does not hear it.

triggers.how: elsewhere the Quran says 'no ḥaraj on the sick' (24:61, 48:17)
the sick-or-traveller pair recurs in rulings (2:184, 2:185, 4:43)

findings.statement: The sick and the traveller are the Quran's standing pair for concession, and the sick are the ones the Quran most often declares free of ḥaraj. Naming them here already points to the closing 'God does not want to lay ḥaraj on you'.
findings.perceptible: The list of conditions and the final purpose clause are one thought. The closing sentence of the ayah is set up by its first exception.

triggers.how: travel as the place where means fail (cf. 2:283: travel, and no scribe found)
B001: uncovering, removing a covering, sweeping; B002: dawn brightening

findings.statement: Being 'on a journey' is the literal condition, and the root's image of uncovering, of open, exposed ground, sets the traveller on bare land where water is not at hand but earth is.
findings.perceptible: The traveller is pictured out in the open. That is why the remedy is the surface of the land itself.

triggers.how: ص ع د B001 rising / B004 surface of the earth: the opposite pole
'comes from' the hollow: movement out and up
B002 sinking or plunging into something

findings.statement: 'Comes from al-ghāʾiṭ' means has relieved himself, and it names the act by its place, a low, sunken stretch of ground. The remedy is the ṣaʿīd, the raised, exposed face of the earth.
findings.perceptible: The ayah moves vertically. A person climbs out of the hollow and aims for the high clean surface, so the path from impurity to purity is drawn as a movement across the terrain.

triggers.how: the other conditions are in the plural 'you'

findings.statement: Every condition is addressed to 'you' (plural) except this one, which switches to 'one of you comes from the low ground'.
findings.perceptible: The ayah speaks of the most private act in the third person singular and names it by a place. Its reticence is audible in the grammar.

triggers.how: the other party of the touching
B001 skin contact, B003 euphemism for intercourse

findings.statement: The ayah names contact with women as touching (lams). The Form III lāmastum (mutual touching) leans toward intercourse, and the mutawātir Form I lamastum can also hold plain skin contact. Both keep the plain sense of a contact that calls for purification.
findings.perceptible: The condition is put in the language of the skin. The remedy uses the same organ, the hand on the skin, with water or earth.

triggers.how: the good things made lawful in 5:4–5: food, then chaste women
the consequence of eating
the consequence of marriage
B003 istiṭāba: cleansing oneself of filth

findings.statement: The earth one aims for is ṭayyib, 'clean, good'. The same word just named the lawful food and, beside it, the marriage of 5:4–5, and the dictionary knows 'the two good things' (al-aṭyabān) as eating and marriage.
findings.perceptible: The passage has a sequence. The two good things opened in 5:5 (food, women) lead to the two occasions for purification in 5:6 (the low ground, touching women), and those are answered by a third good thing, clean earth. Enjoying what is lawful and cleansing after it form one cycle of the good.

triggers.how: the only other tayammamū outside the purification rule is 2:267, 'do not aim at the bad (al-khabīth) to spend from it'
neighbouring image of those heading for the House

findings.statement: Tayammamū is the ritual 'tayammum', and its root sense is 'aim deliberately, single out a target' (as a spear is aimed at one man). Elsewhere the Quran forbids aiming at the bad, and here it commands aiming at the good.
findings.perceptible: Teyemmüm stops being only 'the dust ritual' and becomes a choice of target. The person without water still sets out toward something clean, as the pilgrims of 5:2 set out toward the House.

triggers.how: 'you find no water', and then a verb whose root also names al-yamm, the great water

findings.statement: The act prescribed when no water is found is named from a root that also names the sea (al-yamm), the greatest water.
findings.perceptible: The word itself holds the water that is missing. Lacking water, one does the act whose root also names the sea, and the substitute keeps the memory of what it replaces.

triggers.how: B001 rising, B003 a hard climb or pass; in 18:8 and 18:40 ṣaʿīd is the bare, stripped earth
6:125 pairs ḥaraj with painful climbing (yaṣṣaʿʿadu)

findings.statement: Ṣaʿīd is the face of the earth, open and bare. Elsewhere the Quran uses it for earth stripped of its adornment, and here that bare surface is called ṭayyib and made a means of purity.
findings.perceptible: What elsewhere is desolation (dry ground, slippery waste) becomes here the clean thing one aims for. The same root knows the hard ascent, and God offers the level open surface.

triggers.how: B006: the 'water' of the face, its lustre and bloom
the water's usual Quranic role is to fall on earth and make it good (dominant role, rain reviving land)

findings.statement: The water that washes the face is the water that, in Arabic, also names the face's lustre. When it is absent, the earth that water usually makes good becomes the good thing itself.
findings.perceptible: The usual order (water comes down, the earth becomes good) is reversed in the concession. Now the earth, already called good, comes up to the face in place of water.

triggers.how: travel as the setting of lack
gratitude on little (ش ك ر B002)

findings.statement: 'You do not find water' is the plain lack, and the root's sense of means and sufficiency (wujd, jida) frames it as having no resources.
findings.perceptible: The concession is for the one without means. The ayah answers need, not only absence.

triggers.how: B001: a dense, tangled thicket (ḥaraja), crowding together
ease (rifq, marfiq) set against narrowness
open, level ground against the thicket

findings.statement: God does not want to lay ḥaraj on you: difficulty, and in the root's picture a narrow place or a thicket of trees too dense to pass through.
findings.perceptible: Two landscapes are set side by side: the tangled thicket God does not push the believer into, and the open face of the earth He gives. 'Difficulty' becomes a place one cannot get through.

triggers.how: indefinite noun after min in a negated clause
yurīdu li- + verb: will directed at a purpose

findings.statement: 'Min ḥarajin' after a negation rules out ḥaraj of any kind or amount, and the paired clauses 'does not want … but wants …' set two possible purposes against each other.
findings.perceptible: Not even a trace of constraint is intended. The ayah gives the reason for its law as a contrast between two wills, where a Turkish 'zorluk çıkarmak istemez' sounds milder.

triggers.how: the list of what stays tied (I1)
what is untied

findings.statement: Ḥaraj also means prohibition or restriction (ḥaraja 'alayhi: it was forbidden him). After the lists of loosened and forbidden things, God says He does not wish to add a further constraining knot.
findings.perceptible: The ayah's close belongs to the legal fabric of the window. The purification law is presented as one that loosens rather than tightens.

triggers.how: ص ل و B004: a snare set for game
ح ر ج B009: the hunting dog's share of the game

findings.statement: Ḥaraj also names ropes set for beasts, so 'He does not want to lay ḥaraj on you' can be heard as a refusal to set a snare for those rising to prayer.
findings.perceptible: After the hunting scenes of 5:1–4, the believer is not the game. The law is not a trap laid in the path to prayer.

triggers.how: B005 is glossed الرفق والمهل, the same word as ر ف ق B001
repeated
B003: a scout seeking pasture for the tribe

findings.statement: 'God wants' is plain will, and the root also knows rūd, gentle, unhurried going, and the rāʾid who scouts for pasture for others. God's will here seeks the good ground for the believer.
findings.perceptible: The twice-repeated 'wants' is heard as directed care: a will that looks ahead, finds the clean ground and does not hurry the believer into hardship.

triggers.how: same verb, same object, same 'upon you'
full measure (I10)

findings.statement: 'To complete His favour upon you' repeats 5:3's 'today I have completed My favour upon you', and the completion announced there is carried out here in the ordinary washing of the body.
findings.perceptible: The completion of the religion is not only a historical day. It is brought to fullness again each time a believer washes for prayer, and the grand statement reaches down to the hands and feet.

triggers.how: ḥaraj laid 'upon you'
favour completed 'upon you'

findings.statement: Two things could come 'upon you': ḥaraj, which God does not intend to lay, and His favour, which He intends to complete. The same preposition carries both.
findings.perceptible: The weight settling on the believer is exchanged: not a burden but a favour. The parallel is compositional and disappears when the two phrases are translated differently.

triggers.how: softness against tightness
B011: a land that suits one, where it is good to stay; B012: going on foot

findings.statement: God's niʿma is His favour, and the root's softness (naʿuma: to be soft, easy) makes it the opposite of the narrow, tangled ḥaraj.
findings.perceptible: The closing antithesis is felt as texture: the believer is not pressed into a thicket but set on soft, agreeable ground.

triggers.how: making do with earth in place of water
the lack of water
B003: an udder filling and overflowing (I10)

findings.statement: 'That you may be grateful' is the plain aim, and the root's shakūr is the animal that thrives on a little fodder and the plant that greens at the least rain, as the believer is made whole by a handful of clean earth.
findings.perceptible: Şükür here is not only saying thanks. It is flourishing on little, and the tayammum is its bodily form: the smallest means, fully accepted, is enough.

triggers.how: 'be upright for God as witnesses to justice'
the covenant with Israel: 'if you establish prayer'

findings.statement: Rising to prayer (5:6) is followed by rising for God in justice (5:8) and set against Israel's covenant condition of establishing prayer (5:12). The one verb stands the believer up in worship, justice and covenant.
findings.perceptible: The cleansed person who stands for prayer is the same person asked to stand upright for justice two ayat later. The ablution prepares a posture that goes beyond the prayer mat.

triggers.how: hands stretched out in hostility
hands restrained by God
ي د ي B003: the hand as favour

findings.statement: The believers' hands are washed to the elbows for prayer. A few ayat later other hands reach toward them and God folds those hands back.
findings.perceptible: The same body part is traced through the window: washed, joined in help, stretched in hatred, held back. The ablution gives the believer's hand a place in that story.

triggers.how: B005 includes wiping the afflicted (masḥ dhī al-ʿāha) for blessing and healing
repeated wiping

findings.statement: The hand passing over the head and face is masḥ, the root that gives al-Masīḥ, whom the surah will name repeatedly (5:17, 5:72, 5:75), and that knows wiping the afflicted for blessing.
findings.perceptible: The believer's own wiping hand is a small gesture of the same kind of touch the surah will associate with the Messiah and his healing. The concession for the sick is wiped rather than washed.

triggers.how: idolatrous devices named in 5:3
idol stones

findings.statement: The completion of favour comes through purification. The same root also names the tamīma, the amulet hung for protection, which the plain reading does not invoke but which sits near the divining arrows and idol stones of 5:3.
findings.perceptible: What completes and protects the believer is washing and gratitude, not a hung charm. This is kept as a faint echo.

triggers.how: security after fear in 5:3
trust handed over

findings.statement: 'You who have believed' is also 'you who have come into security and trust', and the purification law is addressed to people already in a pact of safety.
findings.perceptible: The address frames the ritual as an act inside a relationship of trust, not as a test of anxiety.

grammar: فَٱمْسَحُوا۟ بِرُءُوسِكُمْ / بِوُجُوهِكُمْ: wiping takes its object with بِ (contact over a surface), while washing takes a direct object (the whole limb covered with water). Turkish treats both as direct objects.
وَأَرْجُلَكُمْ (accusative) returns to 'wash' across the intervening head-wiping clause; the genitive reading attaches it to 'wipe'.
فَٱطَّهَّرُوا۟ = taṭahharū with assimilated t (Form V, doubled): a deliberate, thorough self-purification, heavier than 'wash'.
جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم: the only condition in the third person singular, a reticent shift inside a plural address.
مَا يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ لِيَجْعَلَ عَلَيْكُم مِّنْ حَرَجٍۢ: مِن before an indefinite noun in a negated clause excludes any ḥaraj whatsoever; yurīdu li- directs the will at a purpose.
عَلَيْكُم ... عَلَيْكُمْ: the same preposition carries the denied burden (ḥaraj) and the intended favour (niʿma).
variants: وَأَرْجُلِكُمْ (genitive, mutawātir; listed under 5:6:21 but it belongs to 5:6:15): sets the feet beside the heads under 'wipe'. The accusative sets them with face and hands under 'wash'. Both keep the feet as the last limb, measured to the ankle-bones.

لَمَسْتُمُ (Form I, mutawātir; listed under 5:6:44 but it belongs to 5:6:35): 'you touched women' can hold simple skin contact. Form III لَٰمَسْتُمُ (mutual touching) leans toward intercourse. Both put the occasion in the language of skin contact, answered by hand-on-skin purification.
structured_output.reread: The believer gets up (body and resolve) and heads for prayer. First comes the face, the part of the body that is turned toward a direction and an intent. Water runs down it and over the hands, up to the elbows, the leaning-joints whose name belongs to gentleness and ease. A hand passes lightly over the head, the top of the body. The feet are washed to the kaʿbs, the ankle-bones that stand out, named by the same word as the raised House the washed face will turn to. Anyone set to one side by janāba purifies themselves thoroughly and comes back from the edge. Then the ayah covers those without water: the sick and the traveller, the Quran's standing pair for relief; the one who has climbed out of the low, sunken ground; the one whose skin has touched a woman's. Having found no water, they aim deliberately at the good, the open, bare face of the earth, and pass the dusty hand over face and hands, the same gesture as the wet hand. That earth is called ṭayyib, the word that has just named the lawful food and, beside it, marriage, so enjoying the good and cleansing after it form one cycle. God's will is set out in two clauses. He does not intend to lay on them any ḥaraj, a narrow place or thicket, or a further knot of prohibition. He does intend to purify them and to complete 'upon them' the favour He declared complete in 5:3. The purpose is gratitude, heard as the flourishing of one who is made whole by a little. The favour completed on that day is brought to its full measure again in every washing, and the upright person standing for prayer is the same person asked two ayat later to stand upright for justice.
